name: Dry needling / acupuncture

lead: Dry needling inserts a thin needle into tight muscle knots, called trigger points, to ease pain. People try it on neck and upper-back muscles that they connect to rounded or hunched posture, and sometimes on the jaw.

The chain is tight muscles needled, less tension in the neck and shoulders, then easier upright posture. Systematic reviews describe short-term pain benefit in some conditions, from small studies with methodological limits. No study examines how posture looks afterward.

paras: A trained clinician inserts needles into specific muscle points for a short period in a session, often as a series alongside stretching or exercise. It overlaps with acupuncture, though the professions dispute how they relate.

Soreness and bruising are common. Rare serious events such as pneumothorax or infection are reported, so it is done by trained clinicians; practitioner scope of practice is disputed in several US states.

chain: Less tension in neck and shoulders
angle.text: People try needling of neck and upper-back trigger points to loosen tight muscles that they connect to rounded or hunched posture. The path runs from needled muscles to less tension to easier upright posture. Short-term pain relief has some support in studies; effects on how posture looks have not been studied.

lead: Dry needling is a technique in which a thin solid needle is inserted into muscle, most often at myofascial trigger points, to treat muscle pain and tightness. Clinicians such as physical therapists use it on the neck, shoulders, upper back and sometimes the jaw muscles, and people who connect those muscles with posture or tension in the face and neck are the ones who bring it up in appearance discussions [1][2][3].

The chain people describe is indirect: release tight muscle, ease pain and stiffness, and move or train more comfortably, which supports posture and the shoulders-and-neck line. Practitioners say the needle disrupts the trigger point and provokes a local twitch response that relaxes the muscle [1][2]. It is distinct in theory from acupuncture, though both use similar needles and the relationship is disputed between professions [2][4].

Systematic reviews describe short-term pain benefits in some conditions but note small, low-quality studies and methodological flaws, and the evidence for long-term benefit is limited [1][5][6][7]. No study found measures facial or postural appearance as an outcome. Gym forums such as T Nation have threads where lifters mention dry needling from physiotherapists for shoulder and back tightness [8][9].

paras: A filiform needle is inserted into skin and muscle without injecting any substance, in contrast with wet needling that uses a local anesthetic or other agent [1][2]. Wikipedia notes that hollow hypodermic needles are also used [2]. Clinicians often aim to elicit a local twitch response, a brief involuntary contraction of the muscle band, which the article says indicates correct needle placement [1][2].

The American Physical Therapy Association says it should not be used alone but alongside manual therapy, exercise and retraining, according to Wikipedia [2]. Proposed mechanisms include endogenous opioid activation and gate control theory, which are not firmly established [2].

Myofascial trigger points are described as hyperirritable spots in skeletal muscle linked to palpable nodules in taut muscle bands, where compression can cause local tenderness, referred pain or a local twitch response [3]. Myofascial pain syndrome is chronic pain from multiple trigger points and fascial constrictions; Wikipedia describes it as a relatively common cause of temporomandibular pain and lists poor posture among possible contributors [10].

The concept is debated. Wikipedia reports that a 2009 review of nine studies could not recommend physical examination as a reliable way to find trigger points, that a 2015 review in Rheumatology concluded the concept lacks scientific basis, and that proponents Dommerholt and Gerwin rebutted that criticism the same year [3]. A study cited there found the pH around active trigger points dropped to 4.3 and that inflammatory and pain-related substances were higher at active trigger points [3].

Painful muscle knots were described retrospectively by nineteenth-century physicians including George William Balfour and Robert Froriep, and researchers in the 1930s such as Jonas Kellgren studied them [3]. Janet G. Travell (1901 to 1997), who later served as personal physician to President John F. Kennedy, pioneered treatment of myofascial pain with procaine injections and vapocoolant sprays, and with David Simons wrote Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction: The Trigger Point Manual in 1983 [11]. Wikipedia credits that book with the term dry needling; Travell preferred 1.5-inch hypodermic needles and never used acupuncture needles [2][11].

Czech physician Karel Lewit described deep dry needling for trigger points in 1979, reporting that it worked as well as anesthetic injections, which he called the needle effect [2][3]. A 1994 study of upper trapezius trigger points compared lidocaine injection with dry needling and emphasized the importance of eliciting a local twitch response [12]. Yun-Tao Ma, founder of Integrative Systemic Dry Needling, is credited with leading the movement in the US [2].

Acupuncture practitioners often regard dry needling as an adaptation of acupuncture, and in 2011 the Council of Colleges of Acupuncture and Oriental Medicine described it that way. Many physical therapists and chiropractors describe it as a biomedical procedure based on anatomy and trigger point theory rather than traditional Chinese medicine concepts [2]. Several authors have reported substantial overlap between trigger points and acupuncture points, with figures of 91 to 92 percent in some papers [2]; Melzack and colleagues linked the two in 1977 [3].

Wikipedia describes acupuncture as a component of traditional Chinese medicine in which thin needles are inserted into the body, most often for pain relief, and reports that sham needling often produces effects similar to real acupuncture and that scientific investigation has not found physiological evidence for qi, meridians or acupoints [4]. Acupuncture proponents hold that it treats a wide range of conditions [4].
No studies found examining dry needling for appearance outcomes such as posture-related facial or neck appearance. Studies of pain conditions exist.

A 2001 systematic review examined needling therapies for myofascial trigger point pain [13]. A 2013 meta-analysis of upper-quarter myofascial pain reported short-term pain reduction while urging caution because of study flaws [2][14]. A Cochrane review of acupuncture and dry needling for low back pain was updated in 2005 [15]. A 2014 literature review discussed implications for clinical practice guidelines [5]. Wikipedia summarizes later reviews as finding insufficient high-quality evidence for pain and disability outcomes, little support for shoulder pain in 2017 and no clear recommendation in low back pain in 2018 [2].

A 2021 meta-analysis of six randomized trials with 241 participants compared dry needling with trigger point manual therapy for neck and upper back myofascial pain, and found non-significant differences between them on pain, pressure pain threshold and neck disability scores [7]. A 2024 meta-analysis of 17 trials with 979 participants found dry needling advantageous for pain intensity in lateral epicondylitis [16]. A multicentre trial of 120 patients with temporomandibular disorder randomized dry needling plus upper cervical spinal manipulation against splint therapy, diclofenac and joint mobilization [17]. A 2024 systematic review also covers acupuncture and dry needling in the physical therapy of scars [18].

Common effects are soreness lasting a day or two and bruising [1]. Wikipedia lists bleeding and pain as mild effects, and pneumothorax, central nervous system or spinal injury and blood-borne infection among severe ones, with a self-reported survey of nearly 230,000 people finding that 8.6 percent reported at least one adverse effect and 2.2 percent needed further treatment [2]. A retrospective review of 2,910 interventions by physical therapists reported no safety events [2].

Wikipedia notes that trigger points near the salivary glands in the masseter muscle carry particular risk if treated poorly [3]. For acupuncture, Wikipedia reports that serious events include pneumothorax and infection, and that it is generally considered safe with trained practitioners and sterile single-use needles [4].

The US FDA regulates the solid filiform needle as a Class II device under the acupuncture needle designation, which governs marketing rather than who may use it. Scope-of-practice disputes between physical therapists, chiropractors and acupuncturists have reached state boards and courts: Wikipedia describes North Carolina, where the Acupuncture Licensing Board said dry needling is acupuncture, and Oregon, where a January 2014 appeals ruling said the chiropractic board lacked authority to include it [2]. In 2016 the American Medical Association called for training standards comparable to acupuncture's [2].

lore.intro: Dry needling is mentioned in gym and training communities as a physiotherapy treatment for tight shoulders, back and glutes, and in posture discussions as a way to loosen neck and jaw muscles [8][9].

claims.claim: Dry needling releases tight muscles that hold back posture and lifting.
Needling the jaw or neck muscles could improve facial or neck appearance.
Dry needling is the same thing as acupuncture.
The twitch response shows the needle hit the right spot.
Trigger points are a real, findable cause of pain.
Needling is risk-free when done by physios.
